newsitem.title: UK: Labour to woo voters with "Blair, the Movie".
newsitem.headline: Labour to woo voters with "Blair, the Movie".

text.p: Voters still dithering over whether Tony Blair should be Britain's next prime minister are to be wooed by a film showing that behind the confident, smiling politician is a man who has known life's hard knocks.

In the documentary, to be televised on Thursday, a week before the May 1 election, 43-year-old Blair speaks candidly of the two big traumas of his life -- his father's stroke when Blair 11, and the death of his mother 10 years later.
He bluntly recalls that as a teenager, "I thought politicians were complete pains in the backside."

Then he goes on to express his frustration with present-day voters who feel similarly about himself. "You say there is a great new Labour Party that is going to change the world, but you know people are cynical," he says.
Campaign chiefs in Blair's Labour Party who gave journalists a preview of the documentary said they hope its openness and human touches will rally voters to Blair.

A boost in his ratings is desperately needed if one opinion poll published on Wednesday is to be believed. It showed Labour's lead over the ruling Conservatives at just five points, by far the lowest figure of the six-week campaign so far.

Molly Dineen, a British documentary maker celebrated for a warts-and-all portrait of army life in Northern Ireland, spent a month observing Blair to make the movie, the fourth of Labour's five all-channel five to ten minute TV election broadcasts.
"I went in very impressed with Blair, and I came out very impressed, and I am going to vote Labour -- probably," Dineen told journalists who attended the preview.

The film, showing Blair playing tennis and at home in the kitchen with his children, as well as performing political duties, brings in some populist, folksy touches such as his ambition as a child to play soccer for Newcastle United.

But it also recalls more sombre moments -- his realisation, for instance, after his mother's death that life could be short. He recalls thinking to himself: "You had better get on, you have got to do things."
All British parties receive free air time on terrestrial channels during election campaigns, but paid-for TV advertising is banned.
Blair's aides hope the film will repeat the success of a similar one in 1987 showing then Labour leader Neil Kinnock walking in an idyllic clifftop setting with his wife Glenys.
The film-maker on that occasion was Hugh Hudson, director of the British Olympic Games movie Chariots of Fire.
"Kinnock's personal ratings went up 16 points overnight," one aide recalled. "But we were so far behind that it wasn't enough to win us the election."
"This film is completely different -- we have different needs and it is a different election."

Other top film directors commissioned in election campaigns include John Schlesinger who made a promotional film for the Conservatives in 1987 and "Four Weddings and a Funeral" director Mike Newell who came to the aid of Labour in 1992.
